passages.t: Kings not by God, and the calf of Samaria
passages.happening:
An alarm sounds. Put the ram's horn to your lips: a bird of prey hovers over the house of the LORD, ‘because the people have transgressed My covenant and rebelled against My law’ (verse 1). Israel cries out that it knows God, but it has rejected what is good, and an enemy will pursue it (verses 2-3).

‘They set up kings, but not by Me. They make princes, but without My approval’ (verse 4). With their silver and gold they make idols, to their own ruin. The LORD has rejected Samaria's calf, and his anger burns. ‘How long will they be incapable of innocence?’ (verse 5). A craftsman made the calf, ‘and it is not God. It will be broken to pieces, that calf of Samaria’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The ram's horn warned a city that enemies were coming. The word rendered eagle also covers the vulture, and either works: a bird of prey circling its victim. The house of the LORD probably means the land and people of Israel, God's household, not a temple building.

Verse 4 pairs Israel's two great sins, kings and idols. The charge about kings set up without God fits the years after 753 BC, when kings took power by murder, and it may also look back to the kingdom's beginning. When the north broke from Judah about 930 BC, Jeroboam I set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, so that his people would not go to Jerusalem, and told them these were the gods who brought them out of Egypt. The calf of Samaria probably means the Bethel calf, the national shrine of the kingdom whose capital was Samaria, though some think a calf stood in Samaria itself.

The irony is sharp. Israel says it knows God. The calf comes from Israel, made by a craftsman, and it is not God.
passages.later: Jeroboam's words about the calves echo Aaron's at Sinai (1 Kings 12:28; Exodus 32:4). Second Kings names the sins of Jeroboam as the pattern every northern king followed (2 Kings 17:21-22).
passages.hard:
Was the calf meant to be an image of the LORD, or of another god?

Jeroboam presented the calves as the gods who brought Israel out of Egypt, which suggests that they were tied to the worship of the LORD rather than a foreign god, even though the wording echoes Aaron's calf at Sinai. Many scholars think the calves were not meant as images of God himself but as pedestals on which the unseen LORD was thought to stand, as the cherubim above the ark were his throne in Jerusalem. Others think they were understood as images of the LORD, against the second commandment, or that they drew on symbols of Baal, the storm god, and blurred the line between the LORD and other gods.

Hosea's judgment does not depend on settling it. Whatever the calves were meant to be, they had become objects of devotion in their own right, made by craftsmen and credited with divine power. A religion can keep the LORD's name while its practice has become idolatry.
passages.asks: Israel said, in effect, that it knew God, and went on making kings and idols without him. Ask where you have kept God's name over something he did not choose. And ask what you have made with your own hands that you now trust.

passages.happening:
‘For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind’ (verse 7). There is no standing grain, and what sprouts gives no flour. If it did, foreigners would swallow it.

Israel is swallowed up and lies among the nations like a useless pot (verse 8). They have gone up to Assyria ‘like a wild donkey on its own. Ephraim has hired lovers’ (verse 9). Though they hire allies among the nations, God will gather them up, and they will waste away under the weight of the king of princes (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The proverb comes from the farming year, in which what is sown decides what is harvested. Wind stands for what is empty and worthless. The whirlwind is the same emptiness come back with destructive force. In Hebrew, the words for what sprouts and for flour rhyme, tsemach and qemach, so the saying sticks in the ear.

Hired lovers turns the usual picture of prostitution around. A prostitute is paid, but here Israel pays. The payments were tribute to Assyria, beginning with Menahem, who raised a thousand talents of silver from Israel's wealthy men for Tiglath-pileser III. The king of princes may be a play on the Assyrian royal title king of kings.

A wild donkey goes its own way alone. Israel, which thought it was buying safety, is swallowed by the power it paid.
passages.later: Menahem's thousand talents are recorded in 2 Kings 15:19-20. The wisdom books use the same law of sowing and reaping: ‘He who sows injustice will reap disaster’ (Proverbs 22:8).
passages.asks: What a person sows, they reap, and empty things come back as storms. Ask what you are sowing now that you would not want to harvest. And ask what safety you have tried to buy that could end up owning you.

passages.t: Altars for sinning, and a forgotten Maker
passages.happening:
‘Though Ephraim multiplied the altars for sin, they became his altars for sinning’ (verse 11). God wrote the great things of his law for them, and they treated it as something foreign (verse 12). They offer sacrifices and eat the meat, but the LORD does not accept them. He will remember their guilt and punish their sins. ‘They will return to Egypt’ (verse 13).

‘Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces’ (verse 14). Judah has multiplied fortified cities. But God will send fire on their cities to burn their strongholds.
passages.hearers:
Altars multiplied across the land show a religion growing in number while it decays in faithfulness. Altars meant for dealing with sin became places for sinning. The law God had given in writing had become strange to the people who received it.

The return to Egypt is a picture. The people God rescued from slavery will be sent back into it, whether in Egypt itself or in the new Egypt of Assyria. Hosea will say it again (9:3; 11:5).

Israel built palaces and Judah built fortified cities, and both forgot who made them. The fire came in the Assyrian campaigns that ended in the fall of Samaria in 722 BC and, for Judah's fortified cities, in Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BC.
passages.later: Sennacherib came against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them (2 Kings 18:13). Amos used the same refrain against Judah: ‘So I will send fire upon Judah to consume the citadels of Jerusalem’ (Amos 2:5).
passages.asks: Israel's religion grew while its faithfulness died. Ask whether more activity in your faith has meant more love for God. And ask what you have built that has helped you forget your Maker.
